sources.title: Q&A with an Alberta politics expert: Taking the province’s pulse on the eve of the referendum

discussion.body: The switch is about arithmetic. Western Canadian parties of the same kind failed to win seats; working from inside mainstream parties, especially governing ones, skips that queue altogether.

Worth remembering where the tactic was read from: far-right populist movements in the United States and the United Kingdom. A method can travel; whether the movement travels with it is another matter.

items.title: Skip the Party, Take Over a Governing One: Alberta's Separatist Turn
items.body:
Jared Wesley, a professor of political science at the University of Alberta, has been talking about the Alberta independence referendum being held on Oct. 19, and about his work in community town halls across the province, on The Conversation Weekly podcast.

Similar parties have been tried in Western Canada, and they failed to win seats. As Wesley describes it, organisers looked at far-right populist movements in the United States and the United Kingdom and started saying they did not need to start their own political party to make this work. The move instead was to infiltrate mainstream parties, governing ones in particular.

sources.title: Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders

discussion.body: The detail that sticks is the co-defendants' insistence that nobody was forced to die. Mackenzie told parents to starve their children so they could meet Jesus, so “no one was forced” becomes an argument about the definition of force rather than a denial of what happened.

One follower who started attending Mackenzie's church at the age of eight still describes him as his “spiritual father” and says he would never say a bad word about him. That same follower's condition deteriorated in the forest because medication was banned. Devotion that durable is what makes a consent defence sound arguable at all — and what should make anyone suspicious of it.

items.title: Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie convicted of murdering 191 people, nearly all of them children
items.body:
Paul Mackenzie, the leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children. He ordered members of his cult to starve their children to death so that they could “meet Jesus”. His doctrine held that education was forbidden and that modern medicine was “evil”.

Twenty-eight other leaders of the movement were convicted of murder alongside him, and they had all pleaded not guilty, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die. Convictions for murder now sit on the record next to that insistence, which makes the meaning of consent the sharpest thing about the case.

sources.title: Where does all the hardware go? The hidden environmental footprint of AI data centres

discussion.body: Which means a headline like “we recycled a million tonnes” can be perfectly true and still tell you almost nothing about whether any virgin material stayed in the ground.

Fair, but rebound is a second-order worry when the first-order number is 22.3 per cent — most of 2022's e-waste was not even documented, collected and recycled responsibly. Precision about offsets starts to matter once collection stops being the bottleneck.

items.title: Why Recycling a Tonne of Metal Rarely Spares a Tonne of Ore
items.body:
A systematic review of 247 studies found that recycling, reuse and sharing often do reduce demand for new resources, but rarely on a one-for-one basis. Recycling a tonne of metal, for example, does not necessarily prevent a tonne of virgin metal from being extracted.

A conceptual study published this year gives that awkward arithmetic a name: circular rebound effects. Its lens is not simply lost efficiency but the way circular strategies interact with infrastructure, governance, market expansion and demand patterns.

The volumes involved are not small: the Global E-waste Monitor records 62 million tonnes of e-waste generated globally in 2022, of which only 22.3 per cent was documented, collected and recycled in an environmentally responsible manner.

sources.title: Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM

discussion.body: Agentic workloads build on accumulated context as the agent reasons, invokes tools and folds in earlier results. Every new turn resends the conversation history — system instructions, prior prompts, tool results and model responses — so the same growing context is processed over and over.

The gain is conditional: reuse is governed by a configurable KV recompute threshold, and the transfer only helps where it actually clears that bar. It also asks something of the cache — the KV has to survive past the turn that produced it and travel in the reverse direction, coordinated by a KV-cache-aware router.

Worth noting what that coordinator is: a lightweight, stateful control-plane component sitting between the client, the prefill nodes and the decode nodes. It stores only block-location metadata, not KV tensors, and picks that metadata up from the response stream rather than querying the decode node separately — a sensible thing to keep off the data path.

items.title: The KV Cache That Travels Both Ways Between Prefill and Decode
items.body:
In prefill-decode disaggregation, a request is split across specialised nodes: the prefill node processes the prompt and builds its key-value cache, then the decode node retrieves those KV blocks and generates the response. Conventional disaggregated serving moves that cache in one direction only, from prefill to decode, and the AWS Machine Learning team says that one-way flow creates inefficiencies for multi-turn workloads.

After a response is generated, the decode node is still holding KV cache entries for both the prompt and the newly generated tokens. When the next turn arrives, the prefill node cannot retrieve those entries, so it has to recompute the KV projections for the previous response tokens.

Bi-directional KV transfer reverses the direction: the decode node returns previously computed KV to a prefill node on subsequent turns of the conversation. It is unglamorous plumbing, but it decides which node is holding the memory of a conversation.

sources.title: Quebec's reserves of maple syrup almost depleted, says new report

discussion.body: Goulet frames the empty buffer as a demand story: he says it has been exhausted as sales continue to rise. The council representing authorized buyers adds that Quebec syrup is gaining market share abroad, with exports up 9.34 per cent in 2024 over the previous year.

The export picture is less triumphant than 'gaining market share' sounds: in 2026 the rise slowed to 2.48 per cent from January through August, against the same period a year earlier. And nearly 65 per cent of maple syrup exports still go to the United States, so diversification has a long way to run.

items.title: The Maple Syrup Reserve Is Empty, So Quebec's Weather Is the Buffer Now
items.body:
Maple sap yields depend on the weather, so the producers' association set up a strategic reserve to keep prices and supply relatively stable. The head of Quebec's maple syrup producers' association says the province's reserve has run dry amid high demand for the product.

Goulet said at the release of a report on the industry's economic benefits that the reserve has been reduced to zero. He says the industry could lose customers if weather conditions prove less favourable for maple sap flow. He points to the stock shortages of 2007 and 2008 as the example of what that costs.

sources.title: Experimental Facilities

discussion.body: The silence is engineered, not architectural. A dome is a shape; what makes this one usable for measuring noise rather than bouncing it around is the wall of two-foot fibreglass wedges.

That 1993 milestone is narrower than it sounds: the first known free-standing geodesic dome combining sound-blocking and sound-absorbing materials, not the first acoustic chamber. The curious part is how long it took anyone to put a serious silencer inside a dome.

items.title: Why NASA's Jet-Noise Dome Is Lined With 17,000 Fibreglass Wedges
items.body:
NASA Glenn's Aero-Acoustic Propulsion Laboratory is a 65-foot-radius geodesic dome with two jobs: reducing community noise and running aeroacoustic tests on aircraft engines and engine components. Nothing echoes during a test, because 17,000 custom-designed fibreglass wedges — each two feet thick — line the inside surface of the dome and sit on the floor and around the test rigs, absorbing sound rather than reflecting it back.

When the lab was built in 1993, it was the first known free-standing geodesic dome to include materials meant to stop sound passing through the walls and to soak up sound within them.

sources.title: Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car

discussion.body: The two statements sit at very different distances from the same event: police will not say Haines was hit deliberately, while the prime minister was quick to call it an apparent attack. That gap may say more about what each side can responsibly assert right now than about any real disagreement over what happened.

The labelling argument is the secondary story. Some MPs in Canberra are complaining that security arrangements have not changed with the climate, and they warn that if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed, one of the greatest tenets of the country's political culture could now be at risk.

And if the Federal Police are right that grievance, not only ideology, is radicalising people in recent cases, then any threat model tuned to organised beliefs will keep missing the individuals who act without one.

items.title: Police Have Not Said an Australian MP Was Hit Deliberately; the Prime Minister Calls It No Accident
items.body:
Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in Wangaratta, a regional town in Victoria. Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene and a knife was seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack. He had been briefed by federal police, whose counter terror squad is helping state officers investigate, and told the national broadcaster the incident was not an accident.

sources.title: NASA Improves Shock, Vibration Analysis

discussion.body: The quiet benefit here is a workflow nobody has to relearn. Most dynamic environments engineers reach for finite element modelling tools only occasionally and end up re-learning complex steps; a standard template that replaces older tools walks them through vibration profiles and shock conditions faster and more thoroughly.

Credit the judgement rather than the software. The partner's testing covered vibration and stopped there; someone still had to decide shock testing was needed, and that call came from the group. The template only did the what-if comparisons afterwards.

That call matters because of when it happens. Problems found on the ground can still be addressed, but once a rocket leaves the launch pad most cannot be repaired or corrected — which is what makes early identification essential.

items.title: A Rocket for a NASA Mission Got Vibration Testing but Not Shock Testing. Then the Dynamic Environments Group Ran the What-Ifs.
items.body:
Engineers in the Dynamic Environments Group at NASA's Launch Services Program Office at the agency's Kennedy Space Center have streamlined how they ensure spacecraft and rockets can withstand harsh vibration, shock, stress and other physical forces. The software's first outing came while certifying a commercial launch provider's rocket selected for a NASA mission — a partner that supplied vibration testing but not shock testing.

The group determined shock testing was needed, then used a template it had created to run what-if comparisons, visualise structural behaviour and answer questions that would once have required extensive manual modelling.

sources.title: Jaafar Jackson on Playing His Uncle in ‘Michael,’ Losing the Original Third Act and the Upcoming Sequel: ‘My Job Is to Come Prepared’

discussion.body: Two years before a frame of the film was shot, he wrote down a list of goals, and one of them was to beat Bohemian Rhapsody and cross $1 billion at the worldwide box office. Planning a record-setting run while you are still preparing for the part is either enormous confidence or an unusually tidy spreadsheet.

The goals list is the fun detail; the archive is the real story. Songs, demos, journals, rehearsals, three acting techniques — and the voice tackled before anything else, which is the one thing a performance like this cannot fake.

items.title: Two Years of Archives and an Acting Coach: Jaafar Jackson's Prep to Play Michael
items.body:
Bringing Michael to life took two years of preparation before Jackson officially landed the role: he built his own archive of songs, demos, journals, rehearsals and performances, worked with acting coach Angela Gibbs, and immersed himself in Stanislavski, Meisner and Uta Hagen. Nailing the signature voice and tone came first.

As for what comes next, Jackson says he hasn't been told anything concrete, but that whatever decision is made he is more than ready to get back into it.

sources.title: Alberta voters weigh future in Canada

discussion.body: The Constitution is doing a lot of work here: the same document that frustrates separatists sets a bar for departure far higher than anything a protest vote can clear.

The symbolic move still counts for something, though. A nonbinding vote that is the first time the province has put separation to the public — and that Elections Alberta calls its largest electoral event — makes the question hard to ignore even if it is not a plan to actually leave.

items.title: Alberta's Nonbinding Vote Asks Whether to Ask Again
items.body:
Alberta's nonbinding referendum vote on Monday is the first time the province has put the question of separation to a public vote, and Elections Alberta has described it as the largest electoral event in the province's history. Essentially, it is a referendum about whether to hold another referendum.

The first nine questions on the ballot address immigration, access to provincial services such as health care and education, and potential changes to the Canadian Constitution.

Wesley's version of the irony is that separatists frustrated by the inability to change the Constitution are using that as a pretext to leave, while leaving would require changing the same Constitution with a much higher threshold for agreement.

sources.title: How Deepgram optimized voice AI at scale with AWS Trainium

discussion.body: The satisfying part is the direction of the optimization: instead of using the four logical cores a Trainium2 exposes by default, they cut to one physical core per replica so more copies of the model fit — less parallelism inside each copy, more copies overall.

Worth noting how conditional that is. It works because a Nova-3 instance fits comfortably on a single physical core; the eight-replicas figure is a property of this model's size, not a general rule about the chip.

items.title: Eight Speech Models on One Chip: The Core-Splitting Trick
items.body:
For Deepgram, serving efficiency decides how much audio the system can process for a given infrastructure budget, which is how AWS frames the problem in its account of the work.

Each Trainium2 device has eight physical NeuronCores, exposed by default as four logical cores, a setting called LNC2. Because each Nova-3 model instance fits comfortably on a single physical core, the team reduced the number of physical cores per logical core to one, LNC1. That configuration hosts eight model replicas per device, with inputs processed concurrently to maximize throughput per device.

The data-parallel runtime coordinating those replicas is driven by a work-stealing queue, with one thread per replica.

sources.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of bugging conference room planned to fly to Saudi Arabia, prosecutors say

discussion.body: The detention fight is really a fight about geography. Prosecutors say Saudi Arabia has no extradition treaty with the United States as they seek to hold him until trial, which is what gives the framing of him being mere days from absconding its weight.

Geography cuts the other way too, though: the family's tickets were bought more than two weeks before the alleged installation, and the defense calls the trip paternity leave. A departure already on the calendar reads differently from a sudden flight, even if a judge still has to weigh intent.

items.title: Prosecutors Say an Ex-OpenAI Engineer Was Days From Fleeing to Saudi Arabia; His Lawyers Point to a Trip Already Booked
items.body:
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, is charged with secretly installing a recording device in a conference room to glean company details, and was fired from his job at OpenAI, according to a government memo filed Sunday.

In their own filings, his lawyers say he had worked at OpenAI since July 2025 and had bought one-way tickets for his family to Saudi Arabia more than two weeks before prosecutors allege the recording devices were installed. The defense describes that trip as paternity leave: roughly two months in Saudi Arabia after the birth of the couple's U.S.-citizen son.

sources.title: ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Screenwriter on Book-to-Screen Changes and Why Jane Austen Is So Adaptable: ‘She’s Almost Like Shakespeare’

discussion.body: Calling him a love-bomber is a gift to the modern reader: it turns a literary cad into a man who would be caught inside a week on a dating app. The joke lands because the conduct is textbook — the script hasn't needed a rewrite.

Careful, though — the label may be doing less work than the behavior. If the moves are identical to what people experience now, naming them mostly describes conduct readers already recognize, and what he does to Marianne is textbook either way.

items.title: Diana Reid's 'Sense and Sensibility': Willoughby Love-Bombs Marianne, Then Ghosts Her
items.body:
Turning Austen's 400-plus-page novel into a film just over two hours long meant leaving some scenes or characters on the cutting-room floor, so the sisters would have room to flourish.

What struck Reid and her producer was the Willoughby character and his relationship with Marianne: he love-bombs her, she says, and then ghosts her, behaviors she calls identical to phenomena people experience today. The vocabulary around those behaviors has changed, she says, but what he does to Marianne is textbook.

sources.title: Portraits of another life: Nemo Gould

discussion.body: The finished machine may be the least interesting part. The pleasure in work like this is the physical, hands-on experience of making, not the result.
Sure, but the screwdriver isn't the art. What turned into the work was a curiosity about how machines function, grown out of taking apart toys and appliances — the hands are only the entry point.

items.title: Nemo Gould Traces His Kinetic Sculpture Back to a Childhood Discovery About Screws
items.body:
That impulse led him to dismantle everything from GI Joes to household appliances, and it grew into a deep curiosity about machines and how they work.

Eventually it became his art: discarded objects rebuilt into machines that whirr into motion with a life of their own.

A video portrait of him pairs animations with interviews with his father, a fellow artist, and makes a strong case for keeping childhood fascinations alive.

sources.title: DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won't want to

discussion.body: Big-company retreat hasn't meant a dead hobby: releases like the Steam Frame and the Pimax Dream Air are still happening, and many of the most interesting developments in the space are now happening on the enthusiast front.

Interesting, but that enthusiast front has a toll booth — a couple hundred dollars of components and a pile of soldering, firmware flashing and 3D printing. The verdict that it stays decidedly niche may reflect how much patience the route selects for, not merely how few people want VR.

items.title: DIY VR: A Couple Hundred Dollars, Soldering, and Firmware Flashing
items.body:
Momentum for alternate realities of every acronym was already in steady decline, and it only dwindled from there. The rate of development of new headsets has slowed, with many companies — Apple among them — scaling back or shelving their efforts.

DIY VR is a thing anyway: a couple hundred dollars in components plus many hours of your time buys a way into virtual reality, bundled with the highs and lows of soldering, firmware flashing and 3D printing. The writer who rode that rollercoaster calls it a decidedly niche movement.

sources.title: Disney found a way to buy Character.AI without buying its lawsuits

discussion.body: Court filings indicate the fall of the chatbot platform was not an accident of the deal but the mechanism of it. Staff and technology move forward; the trouble stays parked in the shell.

The claims don't evaporate with the shell, though. The remainder of Character.AI holds responsibility for those battles and some are still live, which means anyone pursuing them now faces a much thinner company than the one that was sued.

items.title: Character.AI Declared Bankruptcy as Part of a Deal to Hand Disney Its Staff
items.body:
Character.AI declared bankruptcy this week, and court filings indicate the move was itself a key part of a deal: Disney has hired most of the company's staff, including now-former CEO Karandeep Anand, and may acquire most of its technology.

The arrangement also let Disney avoid the beleaguered startup's many legal liabilities and obligations. The deal appears structured so that whatever is left of Character.AI retains responsibility for its legal battles — some of which are still ongoing.

sources.title: AI Proved the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis. What Happens Now?

discussion.body: The detail worth holding onto is the word 'weaker': a machine settling the quasi-Riemann hypothesis has not touched the full Riemann hypothesis, and the two should never be collapsed into one headline.

A batch of 377 announced results tells you about volume, not depth, and the honest way to read a number like that is to find the one item a specialist singles out — which is exactly what happened here.

items.title: OpenAI Announced 377 Results; One Claimed to Settle a Weaker Riemann Hypothesis
items.body:
Among the 377 results OpenAI announced on October 6, 2026, one stood out. That result claimed to settle the quasi-Riemann hypothesis — a weaker version of the Riemann hypothesis, which Quanta calls arguably the biggest open question in mathematics.

Jared Duker Lichtman of Stanford University rated the new proof the most significant AI-for-math achievement so far, by quite a margin — a strong verdict, though it is his assessment of a claim rather than an independent confirmation of the theorem.

sources.title: Ask me anything

discussion.body: Declaring every question acceptable is generous, but the generosity is lopsided: one person absorbs whatever comes at him, while everyone else gets to stay comfortable behind the asking.

That lopsidedness may be the point rather than a flaw, since the film is openly interested in the power dynamics of who gets to ask — and a format where nobody is scolded is one way to make those dynamics visible.

items.title: He Said No Question Was Mean or Crazy — the Film Asks Who Has the Right to Ask
items.body:
Filmed in 2024, as the Netherlands was hardening its stance toward asylum seekers, a short documentary follows Abdulaal Hussein, a Sudanese refugee, as he travels the country holding 'ask me anything' sessions with clubs and groups.

In those forums, locals — most of them white and native-born — are free to ask him whatever they like about his perspective and his life, and Hussein's own ground rule is that no question is mean or crazy or inappropriate.

What the film leaves audiences with is a question about the room rather than the answer: who we are, who we have the right to be, and what we have the right to ask in any given setting.

sources.title: Longtime CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour leaving network after a storied career of 43 years

discussion.body: She didn't give a reason, so the timing has to do the talking. Her exit coincides with a new era at CNN as it comes under a new owner, Skydance — after a yearlong process in which Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6.

Coincidence is not a reason, and her own farewell reads like someone leaving on warm terms: CNN as a partner of 43 fantastic years. What she chose to say instead was “always be truthful, not neutral,” plus a line about looking forward to interesting new projects down the line — which is not the language of a forced exit.

items.title: Amanpour Will Leave CNN After 43 Years — and She Hasn't Said Why
items.body:
Christiane Amanpour is leaving CNN after 43 years, having started there as an entry-level assistant and risen to become one of the most visible correspondents and anchors on television, reporting from war zones and hot spots for decades. She gave no reason for the departure and did not specifically mention changes at the network.

Her daily CNN International show, “Amanpour,” will scale back to once a week at the beginning of 2027 and then end in May, with her leaving the network the following month. Amanpour, 68, also said her PBS show, “Amanpour & Co,” will end at the end of this year.

sources.title: Unifor Stellantis workers in Ontario vote 97% in favour of strike mandate with talks still stalled

discussion.body: Local 444 president James Stewart framed the result as leverage rather than appetite for a walkout — a vote north of 97 per cent across the workplaces, in his words, sends a message of unity and strength. The union itself has said any strike involving these Ontario workers remains a last resort, which is a strange thing to say while holding a 97 per cent mandate.

A mandate is a bargaining chip, not a countdown: without the No Board report, the union can't legally walk out anyway, so the vote's value is mostly at the table. And the table is really about Brampton, where Stellantis has said it plans to sell the plant site to a defence contractor — that's the question the percentage is aimed at.

items.title: Stellantis Workers Vote 97% for a Strike Mandate — With No Legal Strike Position Yet
items.body:
Stellantis workers in Ontario represented by Unifor voted 97 per cent in favour of a strike mandate, as collective bargaining negotiations remain stalled. Unifor represents more than 9,000 Stellantis workers in Canada.

The union says it is not in a legal strike position at this time, because neither side has requested a No Board report — one of the steps labour law requires before job action. A key sticking point has been uncertainty around the Brampton factory, and Stellantis recently said it planned to sell the property to defence contractor Roshel.
